verifiedFacts.claim: In The New York Times oral history, Smith says Lenny Kaye suggested “Gloria” when she wanted another simple-chord song she could riff over, and that its male point of view did not constrain her.

sourceRefs.extract: Patti Smith We had “Land.” Then one day we were in the practice room, making a set list, and I said, “I’d love it if we had another song that had simple chords.” I wanted something I could riff off of. And Lenny said, “Well, there’s ‘Gloria.’” And I was like, “Is that a good one?” And he said, “It’s the best.” It freed me up in a certain way to do a song like “Gloria,” and not be hung up with the fact that it was written from a male point of view.
sourceRefs.label: The New York Times Horses 50th-anniversary oral history (archived 2025-11-10)

verifiedFacts.claim: Smith says “Redondo Beach” began as a poem after an argument with her sister at the Chelsea Hotel and evolved with Richard Sohl and Lenny Kaye into a reggae song.

sourceRefs.extract: Side 1 Redondo Beach [] [] Patti Smith I wrote it at the Chelsea Hotel. I had a rare argument with my sister and she disappeared, I think she went to Coney Island. But I got this frightened feeling that something had happened to her. I wrote it as a poem and I used to read it in poetry readings. And then with Richard [Sohl] and Lenny, it evolved as a little reggae song.

verifiedFacts.claim: Smith recalls the producer, whom she calls John, challenging her to fully commit to improvising “Birdland.”

sourceRefs.extract: Patti Smith I was completely green. I had never worked with a producer. If John couldn’t win, he would step back and challenge me. “OK, you want to improvise ‘Birdland’? You want to wing it? Then really do it.”

verifiedFacts.claim: Smith says “Free Money” was really for her mother and connects it to her family’s severe financial struggle.

sourceRefs.extract: Side 1 Free Money [] [] Patti Smith So many people think it’s a love song. I wrote it as [] “Oh baby,” as if perhaps it is, but it was really for my mother. My family struggled financially, sometimes to the point of not having enough food on the table.

verifiedFacts.claim: Smith describes “Break It Up” as a homage to poetry, Jim Morrison, and dreaming, as well as a document of her friendship and creative process with Tom Verlaine.

sourceRefs.extract: Side 2 Break It Up [] [] Patti Smith The song is a homage to poetry, to Jim [Morrison], to dreaming, but it also is a little document of my friendship with Tom [Verlaine] and our process together.

verifiedFacts.claim: Smith says the word “land” came from Chris Kenner’s “Land of 1000 Dances,” and says she loved “A Thousand and One Nights” and Scheherazade’s successive storytelling.

sourceRefs.extract: Patti Smith The word “land” was from “Land of 1000 Dances” [the 1962 Chris Kenner song]. I loved “A Thousand and One Nights” and the idea of Scheherazade telling story after story.

verifiedFacts.claim: In the “Elegie” section, Smith says she wanted Chet Baker to play at the end, “sort of for Jimi,” but the proposed fee was beyond the album’s budget.

sourceRefs.extract: Side 2 Elegie [] [] Jay Dee Daugherty The music was written by Allen Lanier, who was a skilled musician, and who actually knew things like, you know, scales and notes. [] Chords. [] Patti Smith It really was my dream to have Chet Baker play at the end, sort of for Jimi. But we couldn’t afford him. It was $5,000, but we didn’t have it. I think our whole budget was $20,000.
